Destructive

/dih-STRUK-tiv/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Destructive means causing great and often irreparable damage.

Destructive means causing great and often irreparable damage. The most destructive hurricanes reshape entire coastlines, erasing beaches that took centuries to form.

Worked Example

The invasive beetles reached the island on a shipment of untreated lumber. Within five years they had killed nine of every ten palm trees, and with the palms went the shade crops beneath them and the birds that nested above. Biologists called it the most destructive introduction in the island's recorded history — damage no replanting program could fully undo.

The beetles' damage is massive and largely irreversible — killing nearly all the palms and unraveling everything that depended on them — which is precisely what destructive conveys.

How Destructive Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

ruinous

ruinous: bringing ruin or collapse

catastrophic

catastrophic: involving sudden great damage

Antonyms

constructive

constructive: building up; helpful

harmless

harmless: causing no damage at all

How Strong Is It? — damaging → destructive → annihilating

damaging vs. destructive

damaging vs. destructive: Damaging covers harm of any size, while destructive implies great, often irreversible damage.

annihilating vs. destructive

annihilating vs. destructive: Annihilating is the absolute extreme — destruction so total that nothing remains.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of destructive.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — de-

Prefix — de-: down, undoing (Latin)

Root — struct-

Root — struct-: to build (Latin struere)

Suffix — -ive

Suffix — -ive: tending to

Put it together

Put it together: Destructive is literally 'tending to un-build': Latin de-, 'down,' reverses struere, 'to build.' The same building root gives construct, structure, and instruct. Destiny and distress share only surface letters — their roots are different Latin words entirely.

Use the root in a new word: construct

Use the root in a new word: construct: To construct is to build up — Latin struere, 'to build,' the very root that destructive reverses with de-.

Word Choice

general, strong

Destructive is the heavyweight of this unit's harm words: detrimental harm can be modest and deleterious harm can be subtle, but destructive harm is great, sweeping, and often beyond repair.
